input: How do n-gram embedding tables compare to traditional embeddings in enhancing language model performance?
expected_output: N-gram embedding tables enhance language model performance by storing learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens. This approach allows models to retrieve relevant embeddings during processing, adding substantial capacity with minimal computational overhead. In contrast, traditional embeddings typically represent individual tokens without capturing their contextual relationships as effectively. Studies show that n-gram tables can significantly improve performance, with low-bit precision methods preserving most of these benefits while reducing memory costs. For instance, three-bit n-gram tables can save approximately 75% of table memory while retaining over 99% of the validation-loss improvement compared to models without n-gram embeddings.

3.5 Recovering performance with low-bit training

Compressing the n-gram tables changes the embeddings that the model learned to use, which can reduce performance. We therefore ask whether a short fine-tuning phase can recover this loss, or whether using low-bit embeddings throughout pre-training is more effective. To train with low-bit embeddings, we maintain a BF16 copy for gradient updates but quantize the retrieved embeddings during each forward pass. Both the embeddings and the rest of the model remain trainable, allowing the model to adapt to the chosen precision. We compare four sequences: (1) compress → pre-train, (2) pre-train → compress →fi ne-tune, (3) pre-train → fi ne-tune → compress, and (4) pre-train → compress. Comparing fine-tuning before and after compression tests whether recovery comes from adapting to low-bit embeddings rather than simply receiving more training.

The results are summarized in Figure 6. We observe that a brief fine-tuning phase after compression recovers much of the performance lost at very low precision. After fine-tuning, one- and two-bit tables retain 65.3% and 92.0% of the improvement provided by full-precision tables, respectively. Surprisingly, one-bit embeddings perform even better when used throughout pre-training, retaining 77.0% of the full-precision tables' improvement. This shows that even one bit per embedding component can preserve a large share of the benefit from n-gram tables when the model learns to use them from the start. Appendix C.5 gives the full results, while Appendix C.6 examines how alternative hashing methods affect performance with low-bit embeddings.

3.6 Reinvesting memory in larger tables

Finally, we ask whether the memory saved by compression can support larger tables and improve performance. We use tables with 262k embeddings stored at 16-bit precision as the baseline. We then increase each table to 1M embeddings and test lower precisions to see whether the larger tables can improve performance while using less memory than the baseline. We measure performance relative to the improvement that the baseline tables provide over the model without n-gram embeddings.

The results are shown in Figure 7. We observe that reinvesting the memory saved by compression in more embeddings can improve performance while still reducing total table memory. For example, increasing each table from 262k to 1M embeddings at two-bit precision uses only 52-54% of the original table memory while providing 22-26% more improvement than the original 16-bit tables. Three-bit tables improve performance further while using 77-79% of the original table memory.

We also test a brief fine-tuning phase on the compressed larger tables, following Section 3.5, to assess whether adaptation brings further improvement. Fine-tuning improves performance across all three models, with the largest recovery at one bit: with the same fine-tuning budget, compressing before fine-tuning achieves 97111% of the original tables' improvement, compared with 44-63% when compressing after fine-tuning. At two bits, fine-tuning raises the improvement from 122-126% to 129-145% at the same memory cost. These results suggest a practical approach to memory-efficient deployment: pre-train with more embeddings, then compress the tables and briefly fine-tune the model to recover performance.

Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models

Stephen Chung

Wenyu Du

DualverseAI

Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.

1 Introduction

Recent studies have shown that n-gram embedding tables can improve language model performance with little additional computation [1, 2]. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens. At each position, the model retrieves the corresponding representations to supplement its processing of the text. Because each lookup accesses only a few embeddings, the tables can add substantial model capacity while keeping the computation per token small. This approach has been adopted in DeepSeek's Engram memory, which contains 196 billion parameters in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [3]. However, storing these large tables requires substantial memory, motivating methods that preserve their performance benefits with a smaller memory footprint.

The memory cost arises from the enormous number of possible token combinations. To accommodate them, existing methods map n-grams into a fixed number of table embeddings, allowing multiple n-grams to share the same embedding [1, 2]. Smaller tables force more unrelated sequences to share representations, which can reduce their benefit to the model. Increasing the number of embeddings alleviates this problem but requires more memory. We therefore investigate a different way to reduce table memory: keeping the embeddings while using fewer bits for each embedding value. This also raises an opportunity: if lower precision preserves most of the tables' benefit, the saved memory could support more embeddings and ultimately improve performance.

We propose compressing n-gram embedding tables by storing each value at low precision. At such low precision, the choice of representable values can affect how well the embeddings are preserved. We therefore systematically compare evenly spaced values, values chosen from normal quantiles, and values fitted to the learned embedding distribution using Lloyd-Max quantization [4, 5]. We also examine whether bigram and trigram tables benefit from different precision levels, allowing us to allocate bits according to their sensitivity to compression. Together, these experiments offer practical guidance on choosing quantization methods and bit allocations to balance table memory and model performance.

To test whether these savings extend to large existing models, we also compress the tables in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, saving 47-55% of table memory while largely preserving performance on downstream tasks.

Our main contributions are:

- Substantial table memory savings with little loss of performance. Across three model architectures, three-bit n-gram tables save 80% of table memory while retaining approximately 97% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. We also demonstrate substantial table memory savings in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

- Performance recovery through fine-tuning. A short fine-tuning phase substantially reduces the performance loss from low-bit compression, making aggressive compression more effective.
- Better performance by reinvesting saved memory. Tables with four times as many embeddings, stored at two bits, achieve 122-126% of the original tables' improvement while still using 46-48% less table memory. This shows that reducing precision can enable larger, more effective n-gram memories.

input: How do rVCs differ from bVCs in agent authentication, specifically in terms of roles, capabilities, and issuance authority?
expected_output: rVCs (rich Verifiable Credentials) differ from bVCs (basic Verifiable Credentials) in that rVCs specify additional identity attributes such as roles, capabilities, or authorizations of an agent, while bVCs only encode minimal information, primarily confirming that the entity is an agent without detailing its specific roles or capabilities. rVCs are issued by a designated authority agent within the same security domain, whereas bVCs are solely issued by the security domain's orchestrator. This distinction allows agents with rVCs to engage in more complex interactions and trust relationships compared to those with only bVCs.
context:
s. The latter specify additional identity attributes such as roles, capabilities, or authorizations of an agent. Obtaining rVCs after deployment involves an intra-domain attestation process. For this, a freshly-deployed agent approaches a designated authority agent of the same security domain that is in charge to equip agents with rVCs. The attestation is then accomplished through a dialog where one acts as a rVC requester and the other as a rVC issuer. As a dialog requires mutual authentication, the requesting agent presents its bVCs, while the issuer presents its own rVCs. Once both sides are verified, the issuer creates and hands over the desired rVC, which the receiving agent then stores in its wallet for later use. The conceptual workflow and trust model for one security domain is illustrated in Figure 1.

Figure 1: Conceptual workflow and trust model with deployment (step 1), intra-domain mutual authentication (step 2), intra-domain issuance (step 3) and inter-domain mutual authentication (step 4). The analog workflow in the security domain on the right side is omitted due to the lack of space.

Cross-domain dialogues follow the same mutual authentication process. However, agents from one security domain can't verify bVCs from another due to a lack of the issuer's DID doc. In this case, both agents need to present rVCs that extend beyond the limited information contained in bVCs. A successful verification of rVC requires that each verifier recognizes the issuer of the presented rVCs and inherently trusts it with respect to the claims being made, even across domain boundaries. This type of confidence relationship is named organizational trust as an issuer is trusted to act honestly regardless of its implementation.

VCs are explicitly allowed to carry claims in the form of unstructured data such as natural language text, images, or audio. Since modern LLM-based AI agents are able to produce and interpret unstructured content, they can issue and verify unstructured, schemaless claims about other agents. These novel types of claims can bootstrap automated and dynamic trust establishment in multi-agent and cross-domain ecosystems, as different domains do not need to go through an extensive standardization process to reach an agreement on a common rigid VC schema.

5 Implementation

To demonstrate the technical feasibility, we implemented an exemplary multi-agent system in which LLM-based agents authenticate each other across domains using DIDs and VCs as described above. The setup consists of two security domains, each comprising two LLM-based agents. The LLMs used in the prototype are provided by OpenAI 4 . Within one domain, the agents are implemented using LangChain 5 , while their counterparts in the other domain are realized with AutoGen 6 . This choice of employing heterogeneous agent frameworks reflects the likely diversity of future multi-agent ecosystems. The main purpose of the setup is to show that two agents from different security domains can mutually authenticate by presenting VCs that have been issued to them by trustful agents within their own security domain. Communication between agents within a security domain is implemented natively with LangChain and AutoGen, respectively, whereas cross-domain interactions make use of the latest A2A protocol.

Each agent is equipped with a dedicated wallet, storing its private key for the associated DID as well as its VCs. For simplicity, the file system serves as the wallet backend, without compromising the expressiveness of the setup with respect to the stated objective. Since cryptographic signing and verification of VCs and VPs cannot be performed by an LLM itself, these functionalities are provided to the LLMs as external tools. These tools create VCs in JSONLD format, normalize them using the URDNA2015 algorithm, and attach an issuer proof in the form of a JSON Web Signature based on Ed25519. VPs are generated analogously, but include a holder proof in addition, with the signature applied over the VP. On the verifier's side, the tools perform the reciprocal process, first verifying the VP and subsequently the contained VC. The tools are integrated into the LLMs via injected function calls in LangChain, while in AutoGen they are exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) 7 . In the latter case, each agent is provided with an MCP tool adapter granting access to an individual MCP server that hosts the required tools.

Figure 4 shows the mean completion time per process and model including the variance. These values can only be interpreted by taking the mean LLM response time at the time of the evaluation as shown in Figure 5, the DID resolution time (caused by querying the ledger), and the execution time into consideration. The execution time was constant. However, the sum of the DID resolution time and the execution time are negligible due to their very small share of the total completion time ( < 1%). 4 Concept

Within our concept, each agent lives in the realm of a security domain and is in control of its own DID and VCs. All agents of a security domain are deployed by a dedicated orchestrator. Each agent's DID is anchored in a jointly operated distributed ledger that spans multiple security domains. The ledger is considered to be commonly governed by participants originating from different security domains. It acts as a cross-domain trust anchor for DID docs. Only the agent in possession of the private key associated with a DID is authorized to update its ledger-anchored DID doc, while all agents of the same or different security domain are only allowed to read it. This design ensures tamper-resistant and cross-domain persistence of an agent's identifier and the associated verification material in the form of public keys. So as per definition, each agent has inherent confidence in the operation of the ledger. For secure handling of the agent DID's private key and the VCs themselves, every agent is equipped with a digital wallet.

When initiating a dialogue, agents must mutually authenticate, regardless of whether they belong to the same or different security domains and regardless of the dialogue's purpose, e.g., attestation or service invocation. This zero trust-compliant approach requires each agent to prove ownership of its DID and to present supporting VCs to the other party. The VCs must be cryptographically bound to the DID under investigation. During this exchange, both agents alternate between the roles of a VC holder and a VP verifier: the holder presents its DID and VCs in the form of a VP, while the verifier checks the validity and issuer trustworthiness. If both parties approve the validity of each other's VPs, they are mutually authenticated respectively established trust among each other.

At deployment, an agent receives basic (bVCs) or rich VCs (rVCs), depending on its initial role. bVCs encode only minimal information, such as the fact that the entity is an agent, without specifying roles, attributes, capabilities, or authorizations. They are only issued by the security domain's orchestrator. Hence, a bVC contains the orchestrator's DID as the issuer's identifier. While the orchestrator holds its own DID outside the ledger, its DID doc with its verification material is made available to all agents within its security domain. The purpose of bVCs is to empower freshly-deployed agents to trustfully identify themselves to peers of the same security domain in order to receive rVC

5 Implementation

To demonstrate the technical feasibility, we implemented an exemplary multi-agent system in which LLM-based agents authenticate each other across domains using DIDs and VCs as described above. The setup consists of two security domains, each comprising two LLM-based agents. The LLMs used in the prototype are provided by OpenAI 4 . Within one domain, the agents are implemented using LangChain 5 , while their counterparts in the other domain are realized with AutoGen 6 . This choice of employing heterogeneous agent frameworks reflects the likely diversity of future multi-agent ecosystems. The main purpose of the setup is to show that two agents from different security domains can mutually authenticate by presenting VCs that have been issued to them by trustful agents within their own security domain. Communication between agents within a security domain is implemented natively with LangChain and AutoGen, respectively, whereas cross-domain interactions make use of the latest A2A protocol.

Each agent is equipped with a dedicated wallet, storing its private key for the associated DID as well as its VCs. For simplicity, the file system serves as the wallet backend, without compromising the expressiveness of the setup with respect to the stated objective. Since cryptographic signing and verification of VCs and VPs cannot be performed by an LLM itself, these functionalities are provided to the LLMs as external tools. These tools create VCs in JSONLD format, normalize them using the URDNA2015 algorithm, and attach an issuer proof in the form of a JSON Web Signature based on Ed25519. VPs are generated analogously, but include a holder proof in addition, with the signature applied over the VP. On the verifier's side, the tools perform the reciprocal process, first verifying the VP and subsequently the contained VC. The tools are integrated into the LLMs via injected function calls in LangChain, while in AutoGen they are exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) 7 . In the latter case, each agent is provided with an MCP tool adapter granting access to an individual MCP server that hosts the required tools.

Abstract:

A fundamental limitation of current LLM-based AI agents is their inability to build differentiated trust among each other at the onset of an agent-to-agent dialogue. However, autonomous and interoperable trust establishment becomes essential once agents start to operate beyond isolated environments and engage in dialogues across individual or organizational boundaries. A promising way to fill this gap in Agentic AI is to equip agents with long-lived digital identities and introduce tamper-proof and flexible identity-bound attestations of agents, provisioned by commonly trusted third parties and designed for cross-domain verifiability. This article presents a conceptual framework and a prototypical multi-agent system, where each agent is endowed with a self-sovereign digital identity. It combines a unique and ledger-anchored W3C Decentralized Identifier (DID) of an agent with a set of third-party issued W3C Verifiable Credentials (VCs). This enables agents at the start of a dialog to prove ownership of their self-controlled DIDs for authentication purposes and to establish various cross-domain trust relationships through the spontaneous exchange of their self-hosted DID-bound VCs. A comprehensive evaluation of the prototypical implementation demonstrates technical feasibility but also reveals limitations once an agent's LLM is in sole charge to control the respective security procedures.

1 INTRODUCTION

The advent of LLM-based AI agents has opened new opportunities for enhancing human productivity and decision-making (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). A single agent can autonomously retrieve information, perform calculations, automate workflows, and interface with digital services on behalf of its user. Such capabilities already demonstrate tangible benefits in personal assistance and task execution. However, the true potential of agents emerges when they are able to interact and collaborate among each other across organizational boundaries (Sharma et al., 2025). Through agent-to-agent communication, tasks that exceed the scope of an individual agent can be accomplished collaboratively. For instance, while one agent may support a user in planning a vacation by identifying preferences and budget constraints, it is only through secure and trusted interaction with external agents of travel agencies, airlines, and hotels that the full process of planning and booking a holiday can be autonomously and firmly executed.

This shift from isolated single-agent operation to cross-domain multi-agent collaboration comes with new challenges such as interoperability (Sharma et al., 2025), security (Ko et al., 2025) (Kong et al., 2025) (Schroeder de Witt, 2025), and trust (Huang et al., 2025) (Raza et al., 2025). An important step toward addressing interoperability is the recently published Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol 1 , which provides a standardized interaction layer among agents that remains agnostic to the underlying agent frameworks. Enhanced with payment capabilities as introduced by Vaziry et al. (Vaziry et al., 2025) and later implemented by AP2 2 , it may mark the start of agents to become economic actors. In terms of security, A2A builds upon well-established and widely deployed mechanisms from the Web ecosystem, e.g., TLS with x.509 certificates or OpenIDConnect (OIDC).

The experimental setup demonstrates the technical feasibility of the proposed approach but also reveals its limitations once the LLM of an agent is in sole charge to orchestrate security-related procedures. This design decision led to an improvable completion rate for all tested LLMs. It is also the root cause of an increased LLM usage which in turn extends the procedures' duration significantly and results in increased costs. While this design decision helps to gain interesting insights of an LLM as the controller of a security procedure, its practical applicability is at least questionable if only because in one evaluation run both agents agreed to skip the authentication in one direction against the policies stated in the system prompt. However, the evaluation results are strongly dependent on the concrete implementation under study and therefore should not be interpreted as evidence that delegating the orchestration of security procedures to an LLM is fundamentally impractical. As a next step, we plan to migrate the VC/VP routing logic from the LLM to a deterministic component of the agent and let the LLM be in charge to trigger dialogues, to decide whether VCs are shared with other agents based on data protection and privacy policies, and to interpret structured as well as unstructured claims for trust establishing purposes.

input: Examine the role of self-sovereign identities in enhancing inter-agent trust dynamics within decentralized AI ecosystems.
expected_output: Self-sovereign identities (SSIs) play a crucial role in enhancing inter-agent trust dynamics within decentralized AI ecosystems by providing agents with unique, ledger-anchored Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and Verifiable Credentials (VCs). These identities enable agents to authenticate themselves and establish trust relationships autonomously at the onset of interactions. By allowing agents to prove ownership of their DIDs and share tamper-proof VCs, SSIs facilitate secure and spontaneous exchanges across organizational boundaries. This capability is essential for collaborative tasks that require interaction with external agents, thereby overcoming the limitations of isolated operations and fostering a more interoperable and trustworthy multi-agent environment.

Keywords:

Abstract:

A fundamental limitation of current LLM-based AI agents is their inability to build differentiated trust among each other at the onset of an agent-to-agent dialogue. However, autonomous and interoperable trust establishment becomes essential once agents start to operate beyond isolated environments and engage in dialogues across individual or organizational boundaries. A promising way to fill this gap in Agentic AI is to equip agents with long-lived digital identities and introduce tamper-proof and flexible identity-bound attestations of agents, provisioned by commonly trusted third parties and designed for cross-domain verifiability. This article presents a conceptual framework and a prototypical multi-agent system, where each agent is endowed with a self-sovereign digital identity. It combines a unique and ledger-anchored W3C Decentralized Identifier (DID) of an agent with a set of third-party issued W3C Verifiable Credentials (VCs). This enables agents at the start of a dialog to prove ownership of their self-controlled DIDs for authentication purposes and to establish various cross-domain trust relationships through the spontaneous exchange of their self-hosted DID-bound VCs. A comprehensive evaluation of the prototypical implementation demonstrates technical feasibility but also reveals limitations once an agent's LLM is in sole charge to control the respective security procedures.

1 INTRODUCTION

The advent of LLM-based AI agents has opened new opportunities for enhancing human productivity and decision-making (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). A single agent can autonomously retrieve information, perform calculations, automate workflows, and interface with digital services on behalf of its user. Such capabilities already demonstrate tangible benefits in personal assistance and task execution. However, the true potential of agents emerges when they are able to interact and collaborate among each other across organizational boundaries (Sharma et al., 2025). Through agent-to-agent communication, tasks that exceed the scope of an individual agent can be accomplished collaboratively. For instance, while one agent may support a user in planning a vacation by identifying preferences and budget constraints, it is only through secure and trusted interaction with external agents of travel agencies, airlines, and hotels that the full process of planning and booking a holiday can be autonomously and firmly executed.

This shift from isolated single-agent operation to cross-domain multi-agent collaboration comes with new challenges such as interoperability (Sharma et al., 2025), security (Ko et al., 2025) (Kong et al., 2025) (Schroeder de Witt, 2025), and trust (Huang et al., 2025) (Raza et al., 2025). An important step toward addressing interoperability is the recently published Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol 1 , which provides a standardized interaction layer among agents that remains agnostic to the underlying agent frameworks. Enhanced with payment capabilities as introduced by Vaziry et al. (Vaziry et al., 2025) and later implemented by AP2 2 , it may mark the start of agents to become economic actors. In terms of security, A2A builds upon well-established and widely deployed mechanisms from the Web ecosystem, e.g., TLS with x.509 certificates or OpenIDConnect (OIDC).

The experimental setup demonstrates the technical feasibility of the proposed approach but also reveals its limitations once the LLM of an agent is in sole charge to orchestrate security-related procedures. This design decision led to an improvable completion rate for all tested LLMs. It is also the root cause of an increased LLM usage which in turn extends the procedures' duration significantly and results in increased costs. While this design decision helps to gain interesting insights of an LLM as the controller of a security procedure, its practical applicability is at least questionable if only because in one evaluation run both agents agreed to skip the authentication in one direction against the policies stated in the system prompt. However, the evaluation results are strongly dependent on the concrete implementation under study and therefore should not be interpreted as evidence that delegating the orchestration of security procedures to an LLM is fundamentally impractical. As a next step, we plan to migrate the VC/VP routing logic from the LLM to a deterministic component of the agent and let the LLM be in charge to trigger dialogues, to decide whether VCs are shared with other agents based on data protection and privacy policies, and to interpret structured as well as unstructured claims for trust establishing purposes.

By integrating a fan-out prefetcher, NgramRL reduces idle GPU time during training iterations, allowing for simultaneous CPU cache lookups and GPU verifications. Speculative decoding [3, 10] offers a natural solution for improving the efficiency of RL using a small drafter that proposes tokens which the target model verifies in parallel, preserving the target's exact output distribution. However, this mechanism does not transfer cleanly to the RL rollout setting, for two reasons. First, a separate draft model or a set of trained draft heads [2, 12] consumes GPU memory alongside the policy, optimizer states, and KV cache, and must itself be trained and maintained, an added cost precisely where memory and compute are already scarce. Second, such drafters degrade over training. As the policy drifts, a fixed drafter's proposals are increasingly rejected [13], so acceptance falls over exactly the long horizons on which RL runs. To overcome these issues, model-free drafters [7, 18] remove the additional memory cost by reusing tokens from the prompt or a datastore rather than predicting them, but their draft candidates are confined to a single generation, due to which acceptance stays low on the adapting traces that RL post-training produces.

Our key insight is that during RL training, the rollout already contains its own drafter, for free. Because GRPO revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between steps, a prompt's completions are highly repetitive with those generated for it earlier in training. Prior rollouts are thus a self-updating source of draft tokens requiring no extra parameters, no training, and automatically tracking the policy since they are produced by it. This repetition is especially strong for structured tasks, whose outputs are regular by construction, and it arises across rollouts of the same prompt over training, a signal that previous model-free drafters, which draw only on a single generation, cannot exploit [7, 18].

Exploiting this signal, however, raises a systems problem. A model-free cache carries no GPU memory cost precisely because it lives on the CPU, but a naive integration then serializes the CPU lookup with the GPU forward: the GPU stalls on the host every decode step while the next draft is looked up and the step is scheduled. In our measurements this host round trip idles the GPU for nearly a third of each iteration, and the cache lookup is a negligible part of it; the synchronization and scheduling dominate. Realizing the cache's benefit therefore requires co-designing the drafter with the rollout engine so that the host work is hidden behind the GPU, not merely making the lookup fast.

Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt 𝑛 -gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes ( 𝑗, 𝑏 ) , consisting of the accepted draft length 𝑗 and target-emitted continuation token 𝑏 . A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. 3.4 N-Gram Prefetcher

Placing the cache on the CPU keeps it out of GPU memory but serializes the two processors. As Figure 3(a) shows, each decode iteration is a host-device round trip: the GPU verifies the draft, and only once the result is synchronized to the host can the CPU look up the next draft, schedule the step, and launch its kernels, leaving the GPU idle for ∼ 29% of every iteration. The lookup is a negligible part of this gap; the synchronization and scheduling dominate, so hiding the lookup alone is not enough. NgramRL therefore removes the whole round trip with a fan-out prefetcher that prepares the next step's drafts during the current forward.

In contrast, NgramRL maintains a per-prompt n-gram cache that adapts to the policy's changes without retraining, ensuring high-quality draft proposals. Additionally, it employs an adaptive fan-out prefetcher to overlap CPU cache lookups with GPU verification, reducing idle time and improving overall efficiency. This approach allows NgramRL to preserve the output distribution while minimizing training costs, making it a more effective solution for structured generation tasks.

input: How does Link-CBF's per-link clearance guidance compare to Joint-CBF's whole-body safety approach in enhancing robot evasion?
expected_output: Link-CBF's per-link clearance guidance improves robot evasion by extending safety measures to every body link, resulting in higher success rates compared to the Joint-CBF approach, especially when perception is limited. In scenarios with a fixed camera, Link-CBF achieved a success rate of 90% in reset and 89% in deployment, while Joint-CBF dropped to 76% in deployment. This suggests that Link-CBF is more effective under conditions where the robot cannot accurately perceive the whole-body barrier, as it focuses on the most immediate threats to limbs rather than relying on a comprehensive whole-body safety structure that may not be accurately perceived.
context:
soccer ball (top row) and a foam ball (lower two rows).

- No barrier uses the distance-to-core reward r core only ( r cbf = 0 ).
- Link-CBF adds the lightweight per-link clearance barrier r clear as reward guidance (§III-B); this is the configuration we deploy on hardware.
- Joint-CBF additionally trains with the whole-body joint-space CBF module as reward guidance, evaluated without a runtime filter.
- +filter keeps the joint-space CBF as an online filter. 1

Onboard sensing costs only a few points of evasion. Trained with the same Link-CBF reward, the fixed-camera policy ( 90% reset, 89% deployment) is on par with the state oracle ( 88% and 93% ) despite seeing the ball only as a conservative masked depth (Table II). The oracle's best configurations ( 96 -99% ) sit fewer than ten points above the policy we deploy. The fixed onboard camera alone is therefore adequate for evasion; what perception changes is which safety structure works.

With privileged ball states, the strongest safety configuration achieves the highest success rates. The plain distance-tocore baseline is already strong ( 96% -98% across regimes), and the full CBF-RL recipe, with the joint-space barrier kept as its runtime filter, outperforms it ( 98% -99% ). The +filter column is the best mode in every row of Table II: given accurate online ball states, runtime whole-body barrier enforcement achieves the highest success rate at each perception level. This improvement requires ball states that our onboard stack currently cannot supply.

1 The filter reads ground-truth ball states, so running it on hardware would require a highly accurate online ball state estimator that our vision stack does not provide.

Among the modes that run without runtime ball states, the ranking flips. Link-CBF is best on the fixed camera in both regimes (reset 90% , deployment 89% ), above the nobarrier baseline ( 86% in both) and well above the bare JointCBF, which drops to 76% in the deployment regime. LinkCBF extends safety guidance from pelvis clearance to every body link; under the any-link contact criterion, it improves fixed-camera success from 86% to 90% in reset and 89% in deployment. It is therefore the reward we deploy on hardware (§IV-B).

We theorize that the Joint-CBF gap comes from perception: the policy is asked to internalize a whole-body barrier that it cannot perceive accurately enough, and it learns worse evasions instead. Two changes repair this, and both supply the ball information that the fixed camera lacks. Keeping the joint-space CBF as an online filter hands exact ball states to the barrier itself and lifts the fixed camera to 90% -97% . Giving the policy a better view works as well: with an oracleaimed, ball-tracking gimbal, the same Joint-CBF training no longer hurts (deployment 90% versus 76% on the fixed camera) and beats its no-barrier counterpart with the full safety structure (i.e. +filter). This shows that the whole-body barrier succeeds only when the ball is sufficiently observable. Fig. II (top) illustrates this: deployment success of Joint- CBF climbs steeply with ball observability, while Link-CBF stays nearly flat. Therefore, the design implication is that the strength of the safety structure must be matched to the information available. A hardware gimbal aimed by the same segmentation-based focusing stage that already feeds the policy is left as future work. We also compare against prior results reported in SMP [15] with an omnidirectional throw distribution ( 360 ◦ , 8 -10 m, 12 -15 m/s in codebase) with oracle observations. Under this matched setting, PACMAN scores 98 % reset, in line with their reported ∼ 99%.

B. Hardware experiments

We deploy the Link-CBF fixed-camera policy on the Unitree G1 with a head-mounted ZED Mini. On hardware, the perception node replaces the simulator's segmentation with a learned tracker: an EfficientTAM track, initialized from a clicked foreground point, segments the ball in RGB at ∼ 60 Hz, above the 50 Hz control rate, so the masked-depth observation is effectively fresh with each control step. This also gives us the ability to dodge different balls since the tracker can be initialized on any object of interest. An example of dodging a soccer ball instead of a foam ball is shown in the top row of Fig. 4. The tracked object's ZED depth pixels are retained, and all others are set to far range before pooling to the same 16 × 9 stacked-depth observation used in training. Several filters keep this feed conservative: low-percentile pooling preserves the ball while rejecting isolated ZED flying pixels; distance-aware mask-size checks reject masks that are too tall to be a dodgeball at their measured range; and an optional looming gate suppresses tracked clusters whose average depth is not closing quickly enough, preventing a static object or over-sensitive segmentation from triggering dodges. If the track is absent, rejected by these checks, or lost, the policy receives an all-far frame rather than a false incoming ball. Proprioception comes from the robot's IMU and encoders and uses a walk ↔ dodge mode switch to return the robot to a fixed location between throws. No ground-truth ball states, velocity estimates, or runtime CBF inputs are available at any point: the policy reacts purely to the conservative masked-depth feed, exactly as in the fixedcamera Link-CBF cells of Table II. We stress-test this stack by throwing balls at the robot from the front. A throw counts as dodged only if the ball contacts no body link. The policy dodges 19 of 20 throws ( 95% , Table III). Top: estimated barrier value h for each throw; the dashed line is the per-link keep-out shell ( h = 0 ), and the hit (throw 4, red) is shown at contact.

input: Analyze how advanced sensory feedback and CBFs collaboratively improve evasive maneuvers in humanoid dodgeball.
expected_output:
Advanced sensory feedback and Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) work together to enhance evasive maneuvers in humanoid dodgeball by providing critical information and safety guidance. The integration of sensory data, such as depth perception from cameras, allows the robot to accurately track the ball's position and velocity, which is essential for effective evasion.

The Link-CBF approach, which utilizes a lightweight per-link clearance barrier, extends safety guidance beyond just the pelvis to all body links, improving success rates in evasive actions. This method has shown to increase the fixed-camera success rate from 86% to 90% in reset conditions and from 89% in deployment, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-time scenarios.

Moreover, the Joint-CBF configuration, which incorporates a whole-body joint-space barrier, further enhances performance when accurate ball states are available. This configuration achieves higher success rates (98%-99%) compared to simpler models, indicating that the strength of the safety structure must align with the available sensory information.

In summary, the combination of advanced sensory feedback and CBFs allows humanoid robots to make informed decisions and execute evasive maneuvers more effectively, adapting to the dynamic environment of dodgeball.

The critical factors influencing cost-aware abstention in IT ticket routing methodologies include:

1. **Cost Structure**: The asymmetric costs associated with routing decisions—correct routes incur no cost, human triage costs one unit, and incorrect routes cost five units—are fundamental in determining when to abstain from auto-routing.

2. **Classifier Calibration**: The calibration of classifiers, particularly large language models (LLMs), is crucial. Poorly calibrated models may produce high confidence values that do not reflect actual accuracy, leading to costly misroutes.

3. **Threshold Selection**: The selection of thresholds based on calibration data is essential for minimizing expected costs. For instance, a threshold of 0.60 was found to significantly reduce costs and wrong routes in the study.

4. **Evaluation Framework**: A reproducible evaluation framework that separates predictors, confidence estimators, and rejection scores allows for a clearer understanding of the readiness for auto-routing under specific cost models.

5. **Operational Validation**: The need for organizations to estimate their own local costs and validate the framework against real-world data is critical for effective deployment.

These factors collectively inform the decision-making process regarding when to trust automated routing versus deferring to human triage.

expected_output:
The per-prompt n-gram cache enhances drafting efficiency by maintaining separate lookup tables for each prompt, which allows it to capture repetitive patterns in rollouts more effectively than a global cache. This structure leads to higher acceptance rates of draft tokens, achieving 3.05 tokens per step compared to 2.41 with a global bucket. 

Additionally, the cache is continually updated with recent rollouts, ensuring it aligns with the current policy's preferences without requiring retraining. By retaining only a bounded history of recent entries, it balances memory usage and drafting quality, optimizing performance while adhering to memory constraints. This adaptive mechanism allows the cache to respond dynamically to policy changes, improving overall efficiency during training.

Metrics: We report tokens per decoding step (TPS): the tokens committed per target forward pass, i.e. one plus the mean accepted draft length. It is the standard lossless-speedup proxy in speculative decoding and is hardware-agnostic, so the comparison does not depend on a specific GPU or kernel. We report two aggregates: the mean over the full training run, and the mean over the final 30% of steps. We use the final 30% because training has largely saturated by this point and the cache is fully populated, which is where speculative decoding helps the most. We also plot TPS across the entire run, showing how it evolves as the policy trains.

Runtime measurements use a dedicated rig: Qwen3-8B (bf16, batch 64, 𝑘 = 16) on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB), with a 32-core AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9970X host holding the 𝑛 -gram cache and running the lookup/scheduling chain. input: Examine HCPD's role in optimizing item preference alignment for enhanced SID generation via distillation.
expected_output:
HCPD (Hierarchical Collaborative Preference Distillation) plays a crucial role in optimizing item preference alignment for enhanced SID (Semantic Identifier) generation. By leveraging a frozen discriminative recommender as a teacher, HCPD aligns the teacher's and generator's conditional distributions over legal next tokens along ground-truth SID paths. This alignment facilitates the transfer of relative preferences among items, ensuring that the generator effectively captures user-specific preferences based on interaction history.

The theoretical framework established by HCPD decomposes item-level KL divergence into weighted prefix-conditional KL terms, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of item preferences. This approach not only enhances the generator's ability to model inter-item relations but also directly guides SID generation through collaborative preference relations. Experimental results demonstrate that HCPD consistently improves recommendation performance, particularly in prioritizing relevant items, thereby validating its effectiveness in the distillation process.

2 Related Work

2.1 Generative Recommendation

GR uses item tokenization to encode prior knowledge of inter-item relations into SIDs. TIGER [31] pioneered the use of residual quanti- zation in GR to learn semantic codes by reconstructing item content representations. Subsequent research has focused on incorporating collaborative signals into SID and aligning tokenization with recommendation objectives. LETTER [34] introduces collaborative alignment and code diversity regularization, while ETEGRec [22] alternates between tokenizer and recommender updates using alignment objectives. Other studies reconsider how item tokens are organized and represented. ActionPiece [11] learns merge rules over unordered feature sets using co-occurrences within items and across adjacent interactions. SST [26] compresses history-side item tokens into semantic subwords while retaining fixed-length SIDs as generation targets. DECOR [23] preserves token assignments, combines frozen codebook embeddings with learnable collaborative embeddings, and refines token representations through contextual composition. However, the semantic organization of SIDs does not by itself ensure that the generator learns the semantics of complete items and the relations among them.

2.2 Inter-item Relation Modeling

Discriminative recommenders exploit inter-item relations through transition structures, representation geometry, and ranking supervision [13, 18, 38]. In LLM-based recommendation, explicit relation modeling is introduced through attention structures and collaborative supervision. IAM [44] alternates between attention layers restricted to tokens within each item title and across items, separating title semantics from collaborative relations. TCA [20] normalizes collaborative scores over prefix-compatible items and sums the probabilities of items sharing the same next token to construct soft labels for LLM-based item-title generation. Recent work also introduces relational supervision into GR. APAO [42] optimizes prefix rankings with pointwise or pairwise objectives and adaptively emphasizes underperforming prefixes, while GFlowGR [36] incorporates collaborative signals into item-level terminal rewards and guides SID generation through flow balance objectives. However, GR uses discrete SID tokens shared across items as its basic modeling units, rather than continuous representations of entire items or text tokens processed by pretrained LLMs. Relations among complete items must therefore be expressed through token composition and generation, yet the connection between item-level relations and token-level dependencies remains largely implicit in GR models.

2 Related Work

2.1 Generative Recommendation

GR uses item tokenization to encode prior knowledge of inter-item relations into SIDs. TIGER [31] pioneered the use of residual quanti- zation in GR to learn semantic codes by reconstructing item content representations. Subsequent research has focused on incorporating collaborative signals into SID and aligning tokenization with recommendation objectives. LETTER [34] introduces collaborative alignment and code diversity regularization, while ETEGRec [22] alternates between tokenizer and recommender updates using alignment objectives. Other studies reconsider how item tokens are organized and represented. ActionPiece [11] learns merge rules over unordered feature sets using co-occurrences within items and across adjacent interactions. SST [26] compresses history-side item tokens into semantic subwords while retaining fixed-length SIDs as generation targets. DECOR [23] preserves token assignments, combines frozen codebook embeddings with learnable collaborative embeddings, and refines token representations through contextual composition. However, the semantic organization of SIDs does not by itself ensure that the generator learns the semantics of complete items and the relations among them.

2.2 Inter-item Relation Modeling

Discriminative recommenders exploit inter-item relations through transition structures, representation geometry, and ranking supervision [13, 18, 38]. In LLM-based recommendation, explicit relation modeling is introduced through attention structures and collaborative supervision. IAM [44] alternates between attention layers restricted to tokens within each item title and across items, separating title semantics from collaborative relations. TCA [20] normalizes collaborative scores over prefix-compatible items and sums the probabilities of items sharing the same next token to construct soft labels for LLM-based item-title generation. Recent work also introduces relational supervision into GR. APAO [42] optimizes prefix rankings with pointwise or pairwise objectives and adaptively emphasizes underperforming prefixes, while GFlowGR [36] incorporates collaborative signals into item-level terminal rewards and guides SID generation through flow balance objectives. input: Identify the nuanced research inquiries driving the exploration of visual precision and semantic decomposition.
expected_output:
The nuanced research inquiries driving the exploration of visual precision and semantic decomposition include:

1. **RQ1: Fine-Grained Visual Accuracy** - Investigating whether VAD improves visual accuracy compared to scale-matched post-training baselines.
   
2. **RQ2: Semantics of the Attributed Correction** - Analyzing how the decomposition of corrections concentrates visual evidence in the attributed direction while shifting broader linguistic semantics to the residual direction.

3. **RQ3: Effects of Alternative Supervision Targets** - Examining how different supervision targets impact trained accuracy and the support for correct versus incorrect tokens.

4. **RQ4: Generalization of Checkpoints** - Assessing how different post-training algorithms' checkpoints generalize to held-out tasks.

5. **RQ5: Impact of Training Parameters** - Exploring how supervision divergence, regularization weight, and positive-branch cap affect training outcomes. 

These inquiries collectively aim to enhance understanding of visual attribution's role in decision-making and the semantic structure of corrections.

Overall effectiveness. input: Examine the synergistic elements of ExpertFlow that optimize Mixture-of-Experts inference performance.
expected_output:
ExpertFlow optimizes Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference performance through three synergistic components: 

1. **Routing Path Predictor (RPP)**: This component predicts expert activations across all layers in a single forward pass, achieving up to 95% prediction accuracy. This early prediction enables efficient scheduling and prefetching of experts.

2. **Token Scheduler (TS)**: The TS reorganizes tokens based on predicted expert paths, enhancing expert utilization and improving throughput by up to 16.19% through better expert reuse.

3. **Expert Cache Engine (ECE)**: The ECE loads only the necessary experts into GPU memory, achieving a cache hit ratio of 91.96% and reducing GPU memory usage by up to 93.72%. It also incorporates lightweight correction for mispredictions, ensuring efficient expert management.

Together, these elements significantly enhance compute efficiency and throughput, achieving up to a 10× improvement over traditional offloading methods.

1 Introduction

Sparse MoE models [5, 8, 14, 25] scale parameter size efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts per input, reducing pertoken computation while keeping accuracy comparable to dense LLMs [10, 21, 22]. This efficiency, however, increases memory usage. For instance, Mixtral-8 × 7B [14] requires more than 96 GB of GPU memory, exceeding the 80 GB capacity of an NVIDIA A100 GPU. Although 45.1B of its 46.7B parameters belong to expert modules, only a small fraction is used per input, leading to substantial memory redundancy. This sparsity suggests that offloading inactive experts to CPU and loading only the needed ones can reduce GPU memory demand. Existing studies have investigated such offloading methods [6, 7, 12, 15, 27, 35], but remain limited by three challenges.

Low expert utilization. In the decoding phase, the token distribution across experts can be highly imbalanced, and some experts may receive only a single token. Since expert kernels have nearconstant cost when handling a small number of tokens [32], such sparse assignments lead to low compute efficiency.

Inefficient expert prediction. Early and accurate expert activation prediction underpins effective offloading, as it enables scheduling and prefetching before experts are required. Prior work takes two routes. Regression-based methods [6, 12] approximate router scores, but even small score errors can affect output quality, necessitating extensive fine-tuning to recover the original routing. Learning-based predictors (e.g., ProMoE [27]) improve accuracy, yet their layer-by-layer sequential design reveals expert usage only after the previous layer executes, restricting scheduling flexibility.

The commonly used LRU policy [7] evicts experts purely by recency and overlooks routing patterns, leading to unstable cache hit rates under MoE's dynamic activations. The contribution of our proposed ExpertFlow is orthogonal to this direction, and ExpertFlow can be seamlessly integrated with these techniques to further reduce GPU memory cost during MoE inference.

2.3 Model Offloading

Model offloading reduces GPU memory usage by moving model states or computations to cheaper storage or processing units. Early work such as ZeRO [23, 24] offloaded optimizer states, gradients, and weights to CPUs or SSDs during training, and later extensions applied similar ideas to inference [3, 26, 28]. FlexGen [26] uses a zigzag block schedule to offload activations and KV caches, allowing large models like OPT-175B [37] to run on a single 16GB GPU, while Lamina [3] improves efficiency by shifting attention computation to CPUs. However, these methods are designed for dense LLMs and do not handle the dynamic, input-dependent routing of MoE models. Existing MoE offloading approaches either rely on low-accuracy heuristics [7, 17] or require costly predictor training [6, 12], limiting practical adoption. In contrast, we develop a unified system that provides accurate and low-cost expert routing prediction, enabling more efficient and flexible MoE inference.

3 Method

3.1 System Design Overview

Deploying MoE models under tight memory budgets, such as singleGPU settings, is challenging due to dynamic expert routing, low expert utilization, and heavy parameter movement. These issues are interdependent: inaccurate routing prediction limits scheduling, fragmented token batches activate unnecessary experts, and poor memory planning amplifies transfer overhead. ExpertFlow addresses these challenges through a unified design that integrates a routing path predictor ( RPP ), a token scheduler ( TS ), and an expert cache engine ( ECE ). The RPP provides early global routing signals, enabling the TS to reorganize tokens by predicted paths and the ECE to prefetch only the required experts. This prediction-informed coordination jointly optimizes expert execution, data movement, and memory usage, enabling efficient and scalable MoE inference on constrained hardware.

Figure 2: Routing Path Predictor (RPP). Given a batch of 𝐵 sequences, each with 𝑆 input tokens, RPP predicts MoE expert activations across 𝐿 layers and 𝐸 experts in a single pass. It outputs activation probabilities of shape ( 𝐵, 𝑆, 𝐿, 𝐸 ) to support early expert prefetching.

3.2 Routing Path Predictor (RPP)

3.2.1 Predictor Architecture. Existing predictors [12, 27] use MLPs to infer expert choices layer by layer, creating a sequential dependency that prevents early scheduling and prefetching. ExpertFlow replaces this design with a T5-style encoder-decoder architecture [22] (Fig. 2). The encoder embeds the full input sequence, and the decoder generates routing predictions in one pass. We attach 𝐿 lightweight heads to the decoder, each producing logits over 𝐸 experts for a specific MoE layer. This architecture exposes the complete routing plan before the first MoE layer executes, enabling early prefetching and coordinated memory planning.

3.2.2 Predictor Training. The predictor is trained to produce accurate routing paths for all 𝐿 MoE layers, each comprising 𝐸 experts, in a single forward pass. We log each token's expert selections and encode its routing path as a binary matrix 𝑟 ∈ { 0 , 1 } 𝐿 × 𝐸 . 3.3 Token Scheduler (TS)

In the decoding stage, an adverse routing pattern can arise where each small batch activates almost all experts while each expert receives only one token. Fig. 3 (left) illustrates this worst case for a single MoE layer with four experts and two batches of size four: tokens in each batch select different experts, so every batch activates all experts, causing frequent expert swapping and low perexpert workload. To address this, we introduce the Token Scheduler (TS) , which rebatches tokens between two consecutive batches and groups tokens with similar expert selections into the same batch, as shown in Fig. 3 (right). This rebatching reduces the number of active experts per batch while increasing the tokens per expert, improving cache reuse and GPU efficiency.

Together, these components enable efficient expert loading and execution, reducing GPU memory usage by up to 93.72% and improving inference throughput

In the decoding stage, an adverse routing pattern can arise where each small batch activates almost all experts while each expert receives only one token. B. Hardware experiments

We deploy the Link-CBF fixed-camera policy on the Unitree G1 with a head-mounted ZED Mini. On hardware, the perception node replaces the simulator's segmentation with a learned tracker: an EfficientTAM track, initialized from a clicked foreground point, segments the ball in RGB at ∼ 60 Hz, above the 50 Hz control rate, so the masked-depth observation is effectively fresh with each control step. This also gives us the ability to dodge different balls since the tracker can be initialized on any object of interest. An example of dodging a soccer ball instead of a foam ball is shown in the top row of Fig. 4. The tracked object's ZED depth pixels are retained, and all others are set to far range before pooling to the same 16 × 9 stacked-depth observation used in training. Several filters keep this feed conservative: low-percentile pooling preserves the ball while rejecting isolated ZED flying pixels; distance-aware mask-size checks reject masks that are too tall to be a dodgeball at their measured range; and an optional looming gate suppresses tracked clusters whose average depth is not closing quickly enough, preventing a static object or over-sensitive segmentation from triggering dodges. If the track is absent, rejected by these checks, or lost, the policy receives an all-far frame rather than a false incoming ball. PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball

Lizhi Yang, Junheng Li and Aaron D. Ames

Abstract -We present PAC-MAN, a perception-aware CBFRL framework that couples control-barrier safety with deployment-realistic onboard sensing for whole-body humanoid dodgeball. The deployed policy sees the ball only as segmentation-masked depth from a head-mounted camera, while training-time CBF guidance represents clearance to every body link, and an adversarial motion prior regularizes the resulting evasive reflexes. We evaluate on a controlled anylink contact benchmark with seeded throws in two regimes: single throws and a deployment loop in which the robot walks back to its station and recovers between throws. On this benchmark, the policy comes within a few points of a privileged state oracle: a fixed onboard camera alone is adequate for evasion. We find that usable barrier structure depends on perceptual observability: Joint-CBF gives the best performance with accurate ball states, degrades under fixedcamera observations when used only as training guidance, and recovers with a ball-tracking gimbal or privileged runtime filter. We therefore deploy a lightweight Link-CBF policy zero-shot on the Unitree G1 in the real world, where it tolerates imperfect perception, succeeds on 95 % of throws, and uses semantic segmentation to dodge different balls.

I. INTRODUCTION

Humanoid robots operating around moving objects must react within a fraction of a second, and the evasion itself must not cost them their balance. Dodgeball isolates this safety problem in a short-horizon, whole-body setting: the robot must perceive an incoming ball, determine which links are threatened, and coordinate the torso, arms, and legs quickly enough to avoid contact while remaining upright. Humans solve the same problem by keeping their eyes on the ball and moving their whole body out of its path. Recent learning-based controllers can produce dynamic humanoid locomotion [1], [2], whole-body imitation [3]-[5], and visually conditioned skills [6], [7], but reactive whole-body safety from onboard vision remains difficult [8], [9], especially for a humanoid.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) encode collision-free sets and correct unsafe commands, provided the relevant state is available [10]. Onboard perception breaks this convenient assumption: the incoming object may be visible only briefly, may leave the camera field of view, or may appear as a few noisy depth pixels. CBF-RL can move barrier information into policy training [11], but a deployed policy can internalize only as much safety structure as its observations support. The threat representation and the barrier design therefore

The short observation window and whole-body collision geometry make dodgeball a direct test of safety under partial observation.

We present PAC-MAN, a perception-aware CBF-RL framework for humanoid dodgeball. The central question is how much barrier structure a policy can internalize when it receives only deployment-realistic observations. PAC-MAN studies two levels: Link-CBF, a lightweight per-link reward used during training, and Joint-CBF, a stronger whole-body joint-space projection that can either guide training or stay active at test time as a privileged runtime filter. The two levels separate learned barrier-guided behavior from online barrier enforcement.

How well the learned reflex works depends on what perception tells the policy about the threat. The deployed system segments the ball in RGB and masks the depth image down to a compact ball-only observation. An active gimbal, studied in simulation, tests whether keeping the threat in view for longer makes the stronger barrier structure usable. An adversarial motion prior (AMP) regularizes how the humanoid moves, so the evasions come out as crouches, leans, sidesteps, and leaps; the safety structure itself comes from the CBF terms.

B. Projectile threat model

Balls are thrown on an intermittent timer that leaves a recovery window between throws. The default distribution launches from a frontal cone (within ± 25 ◦ of heading, 2-3 m ahead) with a flight time of roughly 0 . 6 s, which sets the reaction window; the aim point leads the robot's velocity. We mix two threat types equally so the policy learns both evasions: a descending ball that falls across the legs (sidestep/step-over) and a low-arc ball that rises to torso/head height (duck/lean). Throw heights are calibrated against a frozen-statue control (§IV) so that essentially every throw is on-target. We partition environments at reset into 20% ballfree standing anchors and 80% ball-thrown evade episodes.

C. Whole-body safety metric

The robot is hit if the ball contacts any body link and falls if the torso orientation, base height, or sustained crouch crosses a threshold. A trial succeeds if neither event occurs within the reaction window. The benchmark reports reset and deployment regimes in §IV; reset success is the primary single-throw metric. This contact-based score is intentionally stricter than measuring the distance from the ball to the pelvis alone: many failures are limb grazes, so a method that only protects the base can appear safe while still being struck.

III. METHODS

A. Safety-guided learning

Abstract -We present PAC-MAN, a perception-aware CBFRL framework that couples control-barrier safety with deployment-realistic onboard sensing for whole-body humanoid dodgeball. The deployed policy sees the ball only as segmentation-masked depth from a head-mounted camera, while training-time CBF guidance represents clearance to every body link, and an adversarial motion prior regularizes the resulting evasive reflexes. We evaluate on a controlled anylink contact benchmark with seeded throws in two regimes: single throws and a deployment loop in which the robot walks back to its station and recovers between throws. On this benchmark, the policy comes within a few points of a privileged state oracle: a fixed onboard camera alone is adequate for evasion. We find that usable barrier structure depends on perceptual observability: Joint-CBF gives the best performance with accurate ball states, degrades under fixedcamera observations when used only as training guidance, and recovers with a ball-tracking gimbal or privileged runtime filter. We therefore deploy a lightweight Link-CBF policy zero-shot on the Unitree G1 in the real world, where it tolerates imperfect perception, succeeds on 95 % of throws, and uses semantic segmentation to dodge different balls.

I. INTRODUCTION

Humanoid robots operating around moving objects must react within a fraction of a second, and the evasion itself must not cost them their balance. Dodgeball isolates this safety problem in a short-horizon, whole-body setting: the robot must perceive an incoming ball, determine which links are threatened, and coordinate the torso, arms, and legs quickly enough to avoid contact while remaining upright. Humans solve the same problem by keeping their eyes on the ball and moving their whole body out of its path. Recent learning-based controllers can produce dynamic humanoid locomotion [1], [2], whole-body imitation [3]-[5], and visually conditioned skills [6], [7], but reactive whole-body safety from onboard vision remains difficult [8], [9], especially for a humanoid.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) encode collision-free sets and correct unsafe commands, provided the relevant state is available [10]. Onboard perception breaks this convenient assumption: the incoming object may be visible only briefly, may leave the camera field of view, or may appear as a few noisy depth pixels. CBF-RL can move barrier information into policy training [11], but a deployed policy can internalize only as much safety structure as its observations support. B. Projectile threat model

Balls are thrown on an intermittent timer that leaves a recovery window between throws. We partition environments at reset into 20% ballfree standing anchors and 80% ball-thrown evade episodes.

C. Whole-body safety metric

The robot is hit if the ball contacts any body link and falls if the torso orientation, base height, or sustained crouch crosses a threshold. A trial succeeds if neither event occurs within the reaction window. The benchmark reports reset and deployment regimes in §IV; reset success is the primary single-throw metric. This contact-based score is intentionally stricter than measuring the distance from the ball to the pelvis alone: many failures are limb grazes, so a method that only protects the base can appear safe while still being struck.

input: Compare the construction methods of uniform, normal-quantile, and Lloyd-Max codebook families, highlighting their unique approaches.
expected_output:
The construction methods for the three codebook families—uniform, normal-quantile, and Lloyd-Max—differ significantly in their approaches:

1. **Uniform Codebooks**: These codebooks distribute K values evenly across the range from -1 to 1. For example, a two-bit uniform codebook would include values like {-1, -1/3, 1/3, 1}. A zero-centered variant, Uniform*, includes zero and uses K-1 equally spaced values.

2. **Normal-Quantile Codebooks**: This method places values at quantiles of a standard normal distribution, concentrating more values near zero. For two bits, a fixed codebook is used with values like {-1, -0.3186, 0.3186, 1}. This approach emphasizes the distribution of embeddings rather than uniform spacing.

3. **Lloyd-Max Codebooks**: These are adaptive and learned from the trained embeddings' component distribution. Initially, embeddings are normalized, and codebook values are initialized at quantiles of the normalized components. The fitting process involves iteratively assigning components to the nearest codebook value and updating the codebook based on the mean of assigned components, allowing for a tailored representation of the embeddings.

Each method has its strengths, with uniform focusing on simplicity, normal-quantile emphasizing statistical distribution, and Lloyd-Max providing adaptability to the specific embedding characteristics.

First, maximum-based scaling matches the largest absolute codebook value to the embedding's largest absolute component. Second, root-mean-square (RMS) scaling uses the embedding's overall magnitude, calculated as s r = √ 1 p ∑ i w 2 ri . Third, error-fitted scaling chooses the scale to minimize the mean squared error between the original embedding and its reconstruction. We compare these choices to examine how scale selection affects compression quality.

After determining the codebook values and embedding scales, we store them together with the low-bit indices in place of the original embedding tables. During inference, the model retrieves embeddings from this stored representation without repeating the fitting procedure.

3 Experiments

3.1 Experimental setup

Models and data. We train five language models from scratch: nanochat with 26M and 50M parameters, a GPT-2-family model with 30M parameters, and Llama-family models with 31M and 322M parameters. By default, each model uses four n-gram tables, comprising two bigram and two trigram tables, with approximately 262k embeddings per table. We train on ClimbMix [10] and repeat each experiment with three random seeds. Appendix B.1 gives the model configurations and training settings.

Evaluation. For each model, we first train two versions using the same experimental setup, one with fullprecision (16-bit) n-gram tables and one without tables. We evaluate both on a held-out validation dataset, and their difference in validation loss measures the improvement from adding the tables. We then reduce the precision of the trained tables and evaluate the model again to measure how much of this improvement remains. We report this as the percentage of the original improvement retained, where 100% matches the full-precision tables and 0% matches the model trained without tables. Alongside this performance measure, we report the percentage of table memory saved. Results are averaged over three seeds, with standard deviations where shown.

3.2 Table memory savings and model performance

We first ask how much table memory can be removed before the model loses the benefit of n-gram embeddings. We compress the trained tables to one through four bits using Lloyd-Max codebooks with fitted scales. To test whether larger tables can tolerate the same compression, we also increase the number of embeddings per table from the default 262k to 1M in the 26M nanochat model and both Llama-family models.

The results are shown in Figure 2. We find that low-bit compression retains most of the improvement at three or four bits. For example, four-bit tables save 74-75% of table memory while retaining more than 99% of the original improvement. However, reducing precision further hurts performance. Two-bit tables save 86-87% of table memory but retain only 85.9-91.0% of the original improvement. Appendix C gives the full results, including one-bit compression.

3.3 Codebook choices and mixed precision

Codebook values and embedding scales. To understand how best to choose codebook values and embedding scales, we compare the three codebook families and scale choices described in Section 2. We compare these choices using two-bit tables in the 31M Llama-family model.

The results are shown in Figure 3a. We observe that choosing an appropriate embedding scale matters more than the choice of codebook. With error-fitted scales, the three codebooks retain a similar share of the tables' improvement (86.36-86.52%), whereas uniform codebooks with maximum-based scaling retain only 58.04%. Lloyd-Max also performs well with simple RMS scaling, retaining 86.19%. Among the three fitted codebooks, Lloyd-Max provides a small additional gain, so we use it as the default in the remaining experiments.

B.2 Training and validation data

Training uses the shuffled ClimbMix release [10], tokenized with an 8,192-token byte-pair encoding tokenizer. We pack documents into sequences of 2,049 tokens, providing 2,048 prediction targets per sequence. The small models train on approximately 500M prediction targets, and the 322M model trains on approximately 1B prediction targets.

We use separate validation datasets to measure final performance. These datasets come from held-out portions of ClimbMix. We remove duplicate validation documents and any documents also present in training or development. The validation set contains 10,240 packed sequences, totaling 20.97M prediction targets. All compared models are scored on the same sequences.

B.3 DeepSeek and Qwen evaluation

For DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, we compress the n-gram tables while keeping the rest of each model fixed. Their original tables are stored at eight-bit floating-point (FP8) precision, which we use as the baseline when measuring table memory savings. We use WikiText-2 validation data to compare precision allocations. DeepSeek has bigram, trigram, and four-gram tables, while Qwen has bigram and trigram tables. For both models, we use Lloyd-Max codebooks with error-fitted embedding scales as the default for evaluation.

To test whether promising allocations transfer beyond the selection data, we evaluate them on held-out WikiText-2, Penn Treebank, and C4. Each corpus contributes 64 windows and 32,768 scored target tokens, with identical windows for the original and compressed models.

We evaluate the models on HellaSwag, ARC-Challenge, and WinoGrande. HellaSwag and ARC-Challenge use length-normalized accuracy, while WinoGrande uses accuracy. We evaluate their full splits of 10,042, 1,172, and 1,267 examples, respectively. Accuracy differences compare predictions on the same examples, with 95% confidence intervals from 100,000 paired bootstrap samples.

B.4 Training and fine-tuning with low-bit embeddings

This section describes the training and fine-tuning procedures used in Sections 3.5 and 3.6.

Training with low-bit embeddings. We retain a BF16 copy of each embedding for gradient updates and quantize the retrieved embeddings in the forward pass. During backpropagation, we treat quantization as an identity operation, passing gradients to the BF16 copy through a straight-through estimator. Embedding scales are fitted on each forward pass, and the Lloyd-Max codebook is refitted every update for the first 100 updates and every 25 updates thereafter.

Fine-tuning details. For the 262k-embedding tables, fine-tuning uses 381 additional updates on unseen training sequences, with 32 sequences per update. All weights remain trainable, using fresh AdamW states, 20 warmup updates, and a learning rate of 0.1 times the original peak.

For the 1M-embedding experiments, fine-tuning uses new training sequences for the smaller models and reuses pre-training sequences for the 322M model.

B.5 Computational resources

The from-scratch experiments run on RTX 5090 GPUs. Small-model training runs take approximately 10-25 minutes on one GPU, while a 322M run takes 6.4-6.8 hours. DeepSeek and Qwen evaluations use four H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism of four.
